blocks.raw: <Tip>Memorize the strain hierarchy: Concrete crushing (0.003) vs. Grade 60 yield (0.0021). If actual steel strain < 0.0021 at failure, the section is overreinforced (bad). If actual steel strain > 0.0021, it is underreinforced or balanced (good). This distinction is the foundation of ductile design.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeList mistakes={[ "Using 0.003 as the steel crushing strain instead of the concrete crushing strain. The strain 0.003 (3 parts per thousand) is specific to concrete, not steel. Steel at 0.003 strain is well into the plastic range and has long since yielded (at ≈ 0.0021). This confusion breaks strain-compatibility analysis.", "Confusing yield strain with ultimate strain. Steel yield strain ≈ 0.0021; steel ultimate strain is much higher (≈ 0.10 or 10% strain). The balanced section calculation uses _yield_ strain, not ultimate strain. Using the wrong value miscalculates the balanced point.", "Assuming overreinforced sections have no strength advantage. While overreinforced sections are less ductile, they do carry higher loads before failure. However, the lack of warning (brittle failure) makes them unacceptable in code-compliant design, especially in seismic regions.", "Forgetting that ductility (underreinforced sections) is a design requirement, not an option. Code requires ductile behavior to absorb energy and provide warning. Overreinforced design is a violation and may not be approved by authorities." ]} />
